_v2: BK 09:27: Doc Assist own four questions, not the casefile questions; label Ask yourself:
tile: Every document in your casefile, with a walk-through beside it. It won't answer for you. It shows you how.

walk.say: Before you read a word of the document, read the line above it. Who made it, when, and why?

walk.step: Read it once, all the way.
walk.say: Start to finish, no stopping. Hit a hard word? Keep going. Then say what it's about in a few words.
walk.say_image: Look in three passes: the title and labels, then the biggest thing, then the small details.

walk.say: Find the words that say it. Your proof is always in the document.
Who would tell it differently? Who isn't in it?
Find it on your Civic Principles card. Does the document uphold it, deny it, or fight over it?

docs.title: North America, 1775 (map)
docs.src: Source: Exploring American History, Globe Book Company (adapted)

steps.question: Who made this map, and when? Is it from the time it shows?
steps.line: Two places to look: the source line under the map and the title on top. Check the year in the title against 1763.
Find the key in the lower left first. It tells you what the dotted line means. Then follow that line with your finger, top to bottom.

steps.question: What does the map show about where colonists could settle after 1763?
steps.line: Find the shaded colonies, then the dotted line. Which side of the line is off limits? Your KEY VOCABULARY names the mountains it runs along.

steps.question: How would a colonist and a Native nation each see this line?
steps.line: Think like a colonist in 1763 who wanted land. Then think like a Native nation living west of the line. Same line, two views.

steps.question: Should a government be able to tell people where they can live?
steps.line: This is about how far a government's power should reach. Start with the first group on your card: How power is built and limited.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 1's questions in your casefile, starting on page 3. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.

docs.title: The British side · Thomas Whately, who wrote the Stamp Act
docs.src: Source: Thomas Whately, The Regulations Lately Made Concerning the Colonies, and the Taxes Imposed Upon Them, Considered, January 1765 (adapted)

steps.question: Who wrote this, what was his job, and how might that shape what he says?
steps.line: He wrote the tax, and now he's explaining the tax. Ask yourself: would he ever call it a bad idea?
Four sentences. Hard words: a national debt is money a country owes. Keep going, then say what it's about.

steps.question: What reason does Whately give for making the colonies pay?
steps.line: His reason is in the first sentence and the last two. Look for what the money pays for, and who is paying right now.

steps.question: Who would argue back, and what would they say?
steps.line: Who actually has to pay for the stamps? Picture a colonial printer or a lawyer reading this.

steps.question: Is it fair to tax people who had no say in the tax?
steps.line: Ask where a government gets the right to tax people at all. Look in the group called Where government's power comes from.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 2's questions in your casefile, starting on page 4. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: The money raised by these taxes goes to pay the costs of defending and protecting the British colonies in America. The colonies have their own governments to pay for, but so does Great Britain. And Britain carries a huge national debt, most of it from a war fought to protect the colonies. Right now, Britain alone is paying it.

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: The money from these taxes pays to defend and protect Britain's colonies in America. The colonies pay for their own governments. But Great Britain pays for its government too. Britain also has a huge national debt (money a country owes). Most of that debt came from a war fought to protect the colonies. Right now, Britain is paying it all by itself.

docs.title: The colonists' side · the Stamp Act Congress
docs.src: Source: Declaration of Rights and Grievances, Stamp Act Congress, October 19, 1765 (adapted)

steps.question: Who wrote this, and who were they trying to convince?
steps.line: The source line names the group. WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW on Day 1 says who they were. Then ask who could get rid of the tax.
Four sentences. Watch for the word consent: it means agreement. Mark it when you see it.

steps.question: What is the colonists' main complaint, and why does it matter?
steps.line: Find the sentence with the word consent. Say it the way you'd explain it to a friend. Then finish: because ___, which means ___.

steps.question: Whose voice is in this document, and whose is missing?
steps.line: The writers owned property. Now think of everyone in the colonies in 1765 who couldn't vote or didn't own property.

steps.question: What principle about consent is this document fighting for?
steps.line: Consent is the clue word. Read the group Where government's power comes from and find the one that matches.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 3's questions in your casefile, starting on page 5. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: The colonists owe the same loyalty to the King as people born in Great Britain, and they have all the same rights. It is the right of free people that no taxes be put on them without their own consent, given in person or through their representatives. The people of these colonies are not, and cannot be, represented in Parliament. The only representatives of the colonists are the people they choose themselves.

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: Colonists are as loyal to the King as people born in Great Britain. They have all the same rights. Free people have a right: no taxes can be put on them without their own consent (agreement). They give that consent in person, or through representatives they choose. The people of these colonies are not represented in Parliament, and they cannot be. The only representatives of the colonists are the people they choose themselves.

docs.title: Paul Revere's engraving · Boston, 1770

steps.question: Who made this picture, and why did he make it?
steps.line: Revere was a Boston silversmith and a Patriot, and he had this print for sale within weeks. What would make people want to buy it?
Read the title across the top word for word first. Then look at the two groups facing each other. Then the small details: the ground, the signs on the buildings, the sky.

steps.question: What story about that night does the picture tell? Point to two details.
steps.line: Read the title again, especially the second word. Then look at the soldiers: are they a mob or a straight line? And look at the man behind them.

steps.question: What might be left out? How would a British soldier tell it?
steps.line: Picture the crowd from the soldiers' side of the street. What would a soldier put in the picture that Revere left out?

steps.question: Should people be free to publish a one-sided picture of events?
steps.line: This is about a freedom a person keeps even when the government doesn't like what they say. Look in the group called What government must protect.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 4's questions in your casefile, starting on page 9. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.

docs.title: The officer's story · Captain Thomas Preston, at his trial
docs.src: Source: Transcript of British Captain Thomas Preston's testimony, from “The Boston Massacre, The British View, 1770,” EyeWitness to History, 2009 (adapted)

steps.question: Who is speaking, where, and what does he need the jury to believe?
steps.line: Before you read, ask: what happens to Preston if the jury doesn't believe him?
Five sentences. Keep track of time: what happened before the shooting, and what he says after it.

steps.question: What does Preston say happened, step by step?
steps.line: Mark each thing he says the crowd did before anyone fired. Then find what he says about the order to fire.

steps.question: Is Preston's account reliable? How would someone in the crowd tell it?
steps.line: Neither side is neutral. Go back to Step 1: who is talking, and what did he want? Then picture a man in the crowd.

steps.question: Why does a fair trial matter, even for someone the public hates?
steps.line: Look in the group called What government must protect. Read each "Look for it when" cue and find the one that fits a trial.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 5's questions in your casefile, starting on page 10. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: I saw about 100 people surround the soldier on guard, with clubs and other weapons, threatening to kill him. When I asked my soldiers why they fired without orders, they said they heard the word “fire” and thought it came from me. Many in the crowd were shouting “fire.” I told the men I gave no such order. My words were: don't fire, stop your firing.

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: I saw about 100 people surround the soldier on guard. They had clubs and other weapons, and they said they would kill him. Later I asked my soldiers why they fired without orders. They said they heard the word “fire” and thought it came from me. Many in the crowd were shouting “fire.” I told the men I gave no such order. My words were: don't fire, stop your firing.

docs.title: Partner A · The Patriot

steps.question: Who wrote this, when, and who was he trying to reach?
steps.line: Paine sold Common Sense as a cheap pamphlet. Who buys a cheap pamphlet in 1776?
Two paragraphs. The first fires question after question at you. The second makes the argument. Read it like a speech.

steps.question: What is Paine's main argument, and what reasons does he use?
steps.line: Paine argues two ways: the first paragraph goes after your feelings, and the second goes after your common sense.

steps.question: Who in the colonies would push back on Paine?
steps.line: Think about who still had a lot to lose from a war with Britain. Then read Document 7.

steps.question: Who does Paine think should govern America?
steps.line: Paine's last three sentences are about who should govern America. Look in the group called Where government's power comes from.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now argue it with your partner. The four questions are on page 13, out loud, no writing.
text: Some people say, “Come, come, we shall be friends again.” But can you still love and faithfully serve the power that has carried fire and sword into your land? Has your house been burned? Has your property been destroyed in front of you? If so, and you can still shake hands with the murderers, you have the heart of a coward.
There is something very absurd in a continent being governed forever by an island. England belongs to Europe. America belongs to itself.

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: Some people say, “Come, come, we shall be friends again.” But think about it. Can you still love and serve the power that brought fire and sword into your land? Has your house been burned? Have you watched your property get destroyed? If so, and you can still shake hands with the murderers, you have the heart of a coward.
There is something very absurd (silly, making no sense) in a continent being governed forever by an island. England belongs to Europe. America belongs to itself.

docs.title: Partner B · The Loyalist
docs.src: Source: Rev. Charles Inglis, The Deceiver Unmasked, 1776 (adapted)

steps.question: Who wrote this, when, and who was he answering?
steps.line: Inglis was a New York City minister, loyal to the King, answering Paine within weeks. Whose minds was he trying to win back?
Four short paragraphs. His first line is a jab at Paine's title. Catch it, then keep going.

steps.question: What is Inglis's argument against independence?
steps.line: Inglis gives two lists: what peace keeps and what war would cost. Find one thing on each list.

steps.question: Whose interests does Inglis speak for?
steps.line: Look at what Inglis says war would ruin. Who in the colonies made their living from those things?

steps.question: What kind of government does Inglis want, and how is it different from Paine's?
steps.line: His last sentence names a kind of government. Put it next to what Paine wants. Then look in the group called Where government's power comes from.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now argue it with your partner. The four questions are on page 13, out loud, no writing.
text: I find no common sense in this pamphlet, only uncommon frenzy.
If we make peace with Britain, the war that has cost so many lives will end. Our trade will still be protected by the greatest navy in the world.

Suppose we break away from Great Britain and set up a republic of our own. What would happen? My blood runs cold when I think of it. The sword alone would decide the quarrel. Our coasts and ports would be ruined, and thousands would be left poor.
America is too large for a republic. A limited monarchy is the form of government most favorable to liberty.

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: I find no common sense in this pamphlet, only uncommon frenzy (wild, out-of-control excitement).
If we make peace with Britain, the war will end. It has already cost many lives. The greatest navy in the world will still protect our trade.

What if we break away from Great Britain and set up a republic (a government with no king) of our own? What would happen? It scares me to think of it. Only fighting would settle it. Our coasts and ports would be ruined. Thousands of people would be left poor.
America is too large for a republic. A limited monarchy (a king whose power is limited by law) is the form of government most favorable to liberty.

docs.title: The Declaration of Independence · July 1776

steps.question: Who wrote this, when, and who was meant to hear it?
steps.line: Think about who needed to hear that the colonies were now their own country. Pick an audience, and give your because.
Three long sentences. Break each one at the commas. The middle one has a phrase you'll see on the Regents: consent of the governed.

steps.question: What does the Declaration say governments are for, and where does their power come from?
steps.line: Read the middle sentence. Find the words "to protect" and the words "get their power."

steps.question: Who signed this, and who was left out of "all men"?
steps.line: Picture the room: who were the delegates? Then reread Day 4's OUTSIDE EVIDENCE box, on page 15.

steps.question: What can people do when a government destroys their rights?
steps.line: Find the sentence that starts "Whenever." Then look in the group called Where government's power comes from, and read each "Look for it when" cue.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 8's questions in your casefile, starting on page 16. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal, that they are given by their Creator certain rights that cannot be taken away, and that among these are Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness. To protect these rights, governments are created, and they get their power from the consent of the governed. Whenever any government destroys these rights, it is the right of the people to change it or get rid of it, and to create a new government.

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: We believe these truths are plain to see: that all men are created equal. Their Creator gave them certain rights that cannot be taken away. Among these rights are Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness. Governments are created to protect these rights. They get their power from the consent of the governed (the agreement of the people). Whenever any government destroys these rights, the people have the right to change it or get rid of it. Then they can create a new government.

docs.title: The Virginia Declaration of Rights · one month earlier, June 1776
docs.src: Source: Virginia Declaration of Rights, June 12, 1776 (adapted)

steps.question: Who wrote this, when, and how is it connected to the Declaration?
steps.line: Check the two dates: June 12 and July 4. Then ask what a writer does with a strong line he's already read.
Two sentences. Trustee is in your KEY VOCABULARY. Read it slowly; every word counts.

steps.question: What does it say about who holds power?
steps.line: The first sentence answers it. Find the two things it says about power and the people.

steps.question: When Virginia said "the people," who did it mean, and who did it leave out?
steps.line: Ask who could vote or hold office in Virginia in 1776. Thread 1 on your casefile cover is a good place to start.

steps.question: What idea does this share with the Declaration?
steps.line: Put the two side by side. Find one phrase in each about where power comes from. Then find that idea on your card.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 9's questions in your casefile, starting on page 17. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: All power belongs to the people and comes from the people. Government officials are the people's trustees and servants, and they must always answer to the people.

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: All power belongs to the people and comes from the people. Government officials are the people's trustees (people trusted to manage something for others) and servants. They must always answer to the people.

docs.title: “Remember the Ladies” · Abigail Adams to John Adams, March 1776
docs.src: Source: Abigail Adams, letter to John Adams, March 31, 1776 (adapted)

steps.question: Who wrote this, to whom, and why might a private letter say more?
steps.line: She wrote this to her husband, not for the newspapers. Read it asking: would she say this in public in 1776?
Two paragraphs. The first is one sentence, and it's a puzzle: read it twice. Who is taking away whose liberty?

steps.question: What is Abigail Adams asking for, and what warning does she give?
steps.line: Find "remember the ladies," then read to the end. What does she say will happen if they're ignored?

steps.question: Whose liberty is missing from the new country's plans, according to her?
steps.line: One group hides in her first sentence. The other runs all through her second paragraph.

steps.question: She uses the colonists' own argument. Which principle is she turning back on them?
steps.line: Go back to Document 3. What did the colonists say about taxes and representatives? Find it on your card.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 10's questions in your casefile, starting on page 18. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: I have sometimes thought that the love of liberty cannot be as strong in those who are used to taking away the liberty of others.

I long to hear that you have declared independence. In the new laws you will make, remember the ladies, and be more generous to them than your ancestors were. Do not put such unlimited power into the hands of husbands. Remember, all men would be tyrants if they could. If attention is not paid to the ladies, we will start a rebellion, and we will not obey any laws in which we have no voice or representation.

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: Sometimes I think the love of liberty can't be as strong in those who are used to taking away the liberty of others.

I can't wait to hear that you have declared independence. In the new laws you will make, remember the ladies. Be more generous to them than your ancestors were. Do not put such unlimited power into the hands of husbands. Remember, all men would be tyrants (cruel, unfair rulers) if they could. If no one pays attention to the ladies, we will start a rebellion. We will not obey any laws in which we have no voice or representation.

before.title: BEFORE WE TALK
before.text: These were real people, and what happened to them shaped the country we live in. Use their names and their words. No jokes, and no comparisons to everyday life.
